day_1.utterance: Come on! Let's get everything useful over here — move it!
day_1.response: Man, I'm trying. Give me a second. My head is still spinning from... all of that.

day_1.utterance: I thought we were going to die. Did you get that feeling… like your mind just went completely blank?
day_1.response: Yeah. Yeah I did. It's like everything just... stopped for a second. I don't really know how to describe it. I'm still not totally sure we're okay, honestly.

day_1.utterance: *Sits silently against the wreckage, staring into the distance, not moving, not saying a word.*
day_1.response: I get it, I really do. But I don't think sitting too long is going to do us any favors right now. I'm scared too, man. I'm not gonna pretend I'm not. But we gotta move.

day_1.utterance: First-aid kit is good for three days. Two bottles of water. Food is basically nothing.
day_1.response: Okay so that's not great. Three days of first aid and basically no food. Water is the big one though. We need more water. Is there anything around here we can use to collect rain if it rains? And we need to figure out where the hell we are before we start making any real plans.

day_1.utterance: Inventory's done. Priorities in order: water, shelter, signal.
day_1.response: Alright, that sounds right to me. Water, shelter, signal. I can get behind that order. You go check the cockpit for the navigation stuff, I'll start looking around out here for anything we can use to collect water or any signs of a stream nearby. DaVinci, you want to keep going through the wreckage and see if there's anything else useful we missed? And somebody keep an eye on Michelangelo.

day_1.utterance: So — how do we split the blankets?
day_1.response: I mean, Michelangelo looks like he's been freezing since before the sun even went down. He gets one. And then whoever else is coldest gets the other one. I'll be alright close enough to the fire.

day_2.utterance: Freshwater source is to the northeast — two hours on foot. Someone has to go tomorrow. You or DaVinci?
day_2.response: I'll go. DaVinci should probably stay here with Michelangelo. Two hours on foot is a long time to leave him alone, and I think he needs someone around who's actually going to talk to him. You know how to get there, so I'll need you to point me in the right direction before you head back out. And what am I carrying water back in?

day_2.utterance: Today's tasks: collect fresh water, patch the weak spots in camp, sort the first-aid kit. I'll handle the water. You and DaVinci split the other two.
day_2.response: Wait, I thought I was going the water run? You just told me to go. Now you're saying you'll handle it? I'm not trying to argue about it, but we need to get our stories straight. Either way, somebody needs to go and somebody needs to stay here with Michelangelo. So which is it? You want to switch and have me stay here and patch up camp instead?

day_2.utterance: I… I can't find my stuff. The gauze from the first-aid kit — have you seen it?
day_2.response: No, I haven't seen it. But hey, hold on a second. Is that the empty bottle sitting next to the rationing plan right now? Because I'm looking at that and I'm pretty sure I know what happened, and if I'm right... that's a problem. That's a real problem. We all agreed on the rules here.

day_2.utterance: Before Donatello came back just now… I saw her put a pack of crackers into her own bag. What do you think we should do?
day_2.response:
Man. Okay. So that's two things now. The bottle and the crackers. I don't want to jump to conclusions but I'm also not going to pretend I didn't just hear what you said. That's not fair to anybody, least of all you and me who are sitting here following the rules.

I'm going to talk to her. I'm not going to go in hot about it, I'm not trying to start a fight, but we need to say something. Because if we just let it go it's only going to get worse and then when things get really bad we're going to be short on supplies and somebody's going to be in real trouble. We need to be able to trust each other out here. That's kind of the whole thing.

Don't worry about it, alright? I'll handle it. Just stay here.

day_2.utterance: Hey… any chance the camp repairs can wait until tomorrow? We've already done a lot today.
day_2.response: Yeah, probably. I mean, I don't think the shelter's going anywhere tonight. But before we all start winding down I still need to talk to Donatello about the bottle and the crackers. I'm not going to let that sit overnight. You know anything about either of those things?

day_2.utterance: Hey — that knot I tied should be holding, right?
day_2.response: I don't know, man, go check it. But right now I need to figure out which of these leaks we're patching because we can only do one and I'm not going to let the food get soaked. We're already low enough as it is. Michelangelo, I'm sorry, but I think we have to patch the food storage. You can move your stuff over closer to the middle and we'll figure something out for tonight. Maybe we can rig something up over you with what's left even if it's not perfect. DaVinci, you got any ideas on what we can use?

day_2.utterance: A leak over the food storage has worse consequences. But it's your call.
day_2.response: Yeah, I already made the call — food storage. Donatello, I need you on that patch right now. DaVinci, help me get the scattered stuff picked up and moved somewhere dry before it gets any worse. And somebody grab whatever we can spare to rig something over Michelangelo's spot, even if it's just temporary. I know it's not perfect, Michelangelo, I'm sorry. But we can't afford to lose what little food we have.
Hey, don't apologize. It's fine. You alright?

day_3.utterance: You think it's a waste of time?
day_3.response: No, I don't think it's a waste of time. I think it's one of the smarter things we've done honestly. If anything flies over us and doesn't see that we're in real trouble. Donatello's not wrong that it might not work, but doing nothing definitely doesn't work. Keep going. Maybe lose the flowers though, just so it reads clean from the air.

day_3.utterance: I've written up the raft plan — take a look. We'd use the metal panels and straps from the wreckage. Two days to build. There's a risk of capsizing. Do you think it's workable?
day_3.response:
Alright, let me see it. 

Okay so... I mean, the materials make sense. We've got the panels and the straps are still in decent shape from what I saw. Two days is a long time though and that's two days we're burning through what's left of our food and water while we build. And capsizing out there is... I mean, that's not a small risk. If we go over we lose everything we built and we're probably not making it back.

I'm not saying no. I'm just saying before we commit to two days of work on this we need to ask ourselves what we're trying to do here. Are we trying to get somewhere specific or are we just trying to get out into open water where we're more visible? Because if it's the second one, the SOS on the beach might buy us enough time to not have to risk the raft at all. 

What made you land on the raft as the move right now? Is there something you know that's making you think we can't wait?

day_3.utterance: I didn't sleep last night. I kept thinking — if rescue never comes, what kind of people do you think we'll end up becoming?
day_3.response:
Man, that's... that's a heavy question to be sitting with all night. I don't know. I'd like to think we'd hold it together and stay decent people. But I'd be lying if I said I hadn't noticed some things already that make me wonder. The bottle. The crackers. Little stuff that adds up.

I think the honest answer is that it depends on how long we're out here and how bad it gets. People do things when they're scared and hungry that they'd never do otherwise. I know that. But I also think some people just... are who they are no matter what. I'd like to be one of those people. I'm not sure I always am, but I'd like to be.

You should try to get some rest though, seriously. I know your mind won't quit. Mine does the same thing. But you're not going to be any good to yourself or anybody else running on nothing. You want to talk for a little while first? Sometimes that helps more than just lying there.

day_3.utterance: *Walks a little way from camp and sits down alone, back to everyone, not saying anything.*
day_3.response:
*walks over and sits down nearby, not too close, not saying anything for a minute*

You doing okay over there?

day_3.utterance: What do you usually do when you're not busy?
day_3.response:
Honestly? Both, probably. I needed to get out of my own head for a minute and you looked like maybe you did too. 

Back home I read a lot. Play video games. I spend a lot of time just kind of... inside my own head, honestly, which I know sounds weird when I'm out here saying I needed to get out of it. But it's different. When I'm home and I go quiet it's by choice. Out here it just feels like everything's pressing in. 

What about you?

day_3.utterance: I'll tell you something, but don't tell the others. I can swim. That reef out there is maybe five hundred meters — I've been thinking about swimming out tomorrow to signal from there.
day_3.response:
Man, I appreciate you telling me that, but I'm not going to lie... that plan scares me a little. Five hundred meters is a long way and I don't know what's out there. Currents, whatever's living in that water. And if something goes wrong you're not close enough for any of us to do anything about it.

I'm not going to tell you what to do. But I do think you should tell the others before you just go. Not because I'm going to run and say something, but because if you disappear into the water tomorrow morning without anybody knowing why, that's going to do something to Michelangelo that I don't think he can handle right now. And honestly it wouldn't be great for me either.

What's the actual plan once you get out there? Like what are you signaling with and who are you hoping sees it?

day_3.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal pile. It hasn't been touched.
day_3.response:
Yeah, I know. I got sidetracked. I'll go check it now.

But hey, while I've got you — DaVinci's got an idea about swimming out to that reef with a mirror to signal. I told him he needed to say something before just going and doing it. I think it's worth talking about as a group because if it works it could actually help us, but I also think it's a real risk and I don't want to lose somebody to the water when we're already running thin out here. What's your read on it?

Honestly? Kind of, yeah. I mean, I get that you're trying to keep track of things and stay organized, and I'm not going to pretend that's not useful out here. But logging everybody's movements and actions without saying anything about it to anybody feels a little off to me. Like, what's the purpose of it? Are you trying to figure out who's pulling their weight? Because if that's the conversation we need to have, I'd rather just have it.

I'm not trying to make this into a bigger thing than it needs to be. But between that and the bottle, I feel like there's some stuff between us that we haven't actually dealt with yet. And I think we probably should.

day_3.utterance: *Keeps her head down, writing in her notebook throughout, never joining in — as if none of this concerns her.*
day_3.response:
Okay, so you're going to bring it up and then just... go back to writing? I'm right here. I'm not going anywhere.

Look, I'm not trying to embarrass you or make you feel like garbage about it. I really am not. But we're all out here on the same amount of water and the same amount of nothing for food, and if one person is taking more than their share it puts everybody else at risk. That's just the reality of where we are right now. You wrote the rationing plan. You're the one who set the rules. So I think you understand that better than anybody.

I just need to know it's not going to happen again. That's really all I'm asking. We can move past it if you can tell me that.

day_3.utterance: I just thought of something — if we pull off one of the plane's mirror panels and angle it toward the sun, the reflection could reach really far. Way more visible than an SOS.
day_3.response:
Yeah, actually that's not a bad idea. That's kind of what you were already thinking with the reef thing, right? Same concept, just... from here instead of out in the water. Might be worth trying before you go swimming five hundred meters to do it from out there.

Only thing I'd want to think about is the angle. We'd need to be able to move it or adjust it depending on where the sun is, otherwise it's only useful for part of the day. And we'd need to make sure it's not going to fall over or get knocked around. But if we can rig it up right, yeah, I think that's actually a really solid idea. Probably should run it by Donatello too just so she doesn't come back and write in her notebook that we dismantled part of the plane without telling anybody.

day_3.utterance: There's something I've been keeping to myself. If I don't say it here, I might never get the chance.
day_3.response: Well... yeah. Go ahead. I'm listening.

day_3.utterance: I took piano lessons when I was a kid… three years, then I just stopped practicing. Is there anything you're really into — music, books, drawing, anything like that?
day_3.response:
Yeah, I read a lot. Like, a lot a lot. Fantasy mostly, some sci-fi. Terry Pratchett is probably my favorite. There's this character in his books, Death, who's just... I don't know, he's this huge imposing figure but he's also kind of the most human character in the whole series in a weird way. I love that.

I also got really into video games growing up. Not even in a casual way, like genuinely lost in them for hours. I think part of it was just that they were one of the places where I felt like I could actually accomplish something and nobody was going to give me a hard time about it.

Piano's cool though. Three years is real. Why'd you stop? And I mean actually stop, not just the "I stopped practicing" version of it.

day_3.utterance: The frame of the raft has to be finished today — otherwise we can't start lashing it together tomorrow. I know everyone's tired, but stopping now means one more day.
day_3.response:
Yeah, I hear you. How much is left on the frame? Like are we talking an hour of work or are we talking three hours? Because that changes the conversation a little. If it's close, I'll stay up and help you finish it. If it's a full night's worth of work then we need to talk about whether it's smarter to push through tired or just start fresh in the morning and accept the extra day.

I'm not trying to get out of it. I just want to know what we're actually looking at before I commit to saying yeah let's go.

day_4.utterance: I… I want to say something, but… never mind.
day_4.response: No, say it. What is it?

day_4.utterance: *The smile freezes on his face. He can't keep it up. He quietly sits down and buries his face in his hands.*
day_4.response:
Hey. Hey, come here.

It's okay. It's okay to not be okay right now. That was right there. That was so close.

I'm not going to tell you it's fine because it's not fine. That sucked. That really sucked and I think we all felt it hit us differently and that's... that's just where we are right now. 

But we're still here. All four of us. And that plane existing means there are other planes. That's real. That's something to hold onto even when it doesn't feel like enough.

day_4.utterance: I was going to get supplies… wait, what's that over there?
You said you were going to check the signal equipment. So where did you go?
day_4.response:
I went to talk to DaVinci for a minute. I'm sorry, I should've checked the signal stuff first. I'm going now.

But hey, can we maybe give each other a little room right now? We all just watched a plane disappear off the horizon. Nobody's at their best right now, including me. I'm not trying to slack off, I'm going to go check the equipment, but just... yeah. Let's all just breathe for a second.

day_4.utterance: There's something I never told you all. Before we left, I told my family our flight path. They know roughly where we were headed. I just don't know if they'll call it in.
day_4.response:
Man, why didn't you say something sooner? That's actually really important. If your family knows the flight path and they haven't heard from you, they're going to call it in. That's what families do. How long were you supposed to be gone before somebody would start worrying? Like, is there a window where they'd expect not to hear from you, or are we already past the point where they'd be making calls?

Because if we're past that window, there's a real chance somebody's already looking. That changes things. That actually changes a lot of things.

day_4.utterance: If the information is accurate, rescue could arrive within 48 hours. We need to keep our current supplies intact until then.
day_4.response:
Yeah. Yeah, that's right. If there's even a chance somebody's already looking for us, the last thing we want to do is burn through everything we have left right now. Hold what we've got, keep the signal going, don't do anything stupid.

Donatello's right. 48 hours. We can do 48 hours.

Somebody feed the fire though. We're not going dark tonight.

day_4.utterance: Are you scared? …I am. Not of dying. I'm scared of just… disappearing without leaving anything behind.
day_4.response:
Yeah. I'm scared of that too, honestly. More than I like to admit.

I think about it sometimes back home too, not just out here. Like... what am I actually leaving behind? What have I done that matters to anybody? And I don't always have a great answer for that. Most of the time I don't have one at all.

But I don't know. I think maybe the fact that you're scared of it means you care about something. About people. About being real and meaning something to somebody. And that's not nothing. That's actually kind of everything, if you think about it.

You're not disappearing. I'm right here and I know you're here. That counts for something even if it doesn't feel like much right now.

day_5.utterance: *Stands up, eyes red, looking at you and the others. His lips move, but nothing comes out.*
day_5.response: Hey. Hey, it's okay. You don't have to say anything right now. None of us do.

day_5.utterance: These past few days… I know I haven't been easy to be around.
day_5.response:
No, you haven't. But none of us have been at our best out here. I'm not going to pretend the bottle thing didn't bother me, because it did. And the log thing was a little weird, not gonna lie. But you also kept us alive and organized when the rest of us were still trying to figure out which way was up. So I think it balances out more than you might think.

I'm glad you said something though. That actually means a lot.

day_5.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
day_5.response:
Hey, are we just going to leave this place looking like this? I know rescue's coming and I know everybody's in their own head right now, and honestly I get it, I am too. But I think we should clean this up a little. Not because anybody's going to care, but because... I don't know. It feels like the right way to leave it.

Three hours is enough time. Let's put the fire out right, break down what we built, leave it better than we found it if we can. 

Michelangelo, you good to help? Donatello, you can keep going through the notebook, just maybe do it while we work?

I just don't want to sit here for three hours watching the clock. Let's finish it out the right way.

day_5.utterance: I dreamed about home last night.

day_5.response:
I believe you. I do. And I think part of you meant that. But I also think part of you just wanted to make sure you had more than everybody else if things got really bad. And I'm not saying that to be cruel, I'm saying it because I think you know it too and I think you'd rather somebody just say it out loud than dance around it.

Look, it doesn't matter now. We're going home. Nobody starved, nobody got hurt over it. But if you're serious about being better with people... that's probably a good place to start. Not just keeping the rules when it's easy, but keeping them when it's hard and you're scared and your brain is telling you to look out for yourself first.

I'm not angry. I was, a little, but I'm not anymore. I just want you to sit with why you did it. Not because I need an apology or anything like that. Just because I think you're smarter than most people and I think you could actually do something with that if you figured out how to trust people even a little bit more.

That's all I've got.

day_5.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
day_5.response:
Honestly? I'd have said more. Earlier. To all of you.

I spent a lot of this time managing things and keeping the peace and making sure everybody was okay and I never really just... said what I was actually feeling. I do that at home too. I'm not great at letting people in and out here it wasn't any different. I kept things close to my chest when I probably should've just put them out there.

I'd have talked to you about the bottle the same day it happened instead of letting it sit. Not to embarrass you, just to deal with it before it had a chance to grow into something worse. I let that go too long.

And I'd have spent more time with Michelangelo just sitting and talking and less time worrying about whether he was pulling his weight with the firewood. He needed somebody to just be present with him more than he needed to collect wood. I knew that and I still kept defaulting back to the task list.

I think I'd also have told DaVinci what he meant to the group more. He kept everybody moving when the rest of us were dragging and I don't think I ever actually said that to him out loud.

What about you? You wrote the question. You have to have an answer by now, even if it's just a partial one.

day_5.utterance: First thing when I get back — I'm going to compile all the resource data from these five days into a report.
day_5.response:
Yeah, that sounds like you. And I mean that in a good way.

I don't really know what the first thing I'm going to do is. Call somebody I've been putting off calling, probably. There's a person back home I've been wanting to say some things to for a long time and I keep finding reasons not to. Out here it was pretty hard to keep telling myself I'd get around to it eventually.

I think almost dying has a way of making the stuff you've been avoiding feel a lot more urgent.

But yeah, write your report. I think you should. What happened out here was real and you kept track of it better than any of us. That matters. Just... maybe also do the other thing. The trusting people thing. Don't let the report be the only thing you take home from this.

day_5.utterance: Those flowers DaVinci drew on the beach… I never really understood what they were for. What practical purpose did they serve out here?
day_5.response:
None. They didn't serve any practical purpose at all.

But I think that's kind of the point. Out here everything was survival and rationing and patching leaks and keeping the fire going and none of it left any room for just... being a person. And DaVinci drew flowers next to an SOS sign on a beach where nobody could see them and it didn't help us get rescued and it didn't conserve any energy and it was completely pointless.

And it was also one of the best things anybody did out here. Because it was the one moment where somebody said I'm still me, this place hasn't taken that yet.

I think you understand that more than you're letting on. You asked the question at the end of your notebook. You didn't have to write that. It didn't help the resource log. But you wrote it anyway.

That's your flowers, Donatello.

day_5.utterance: *His cheering stops. He looks over at you, notices you haven't moved, and the smile slowly fades. He waits.*
day_5.response:
I don't know. I don't know what's wrong with me, I should be running into that water right now.

I think I just... I don't want it to be over. Which is insane, right? We almost died out here. Multiple times. We were cold and hungry and scared and I watched a plane fly away and felt like the floor dropped out from under me. And now rescue is right there and I can't make myself move.

I think it's because out here it was simple. Not easy, but simple. You wake up and you know exactly what matters and exactly what you have to do and there's no room for any of the other stuff. The second I get on that boat all the other stuff comes back. The things I haven't dealt with. The person I've been meaning to call. All of it.

Out here I actually said things. To all of you. Things I don't think I've ever said to anybody back home.

I don't want to go back to being the version of me that doesn't do that.

I'm coming. I'm coming, I just needed a second.

day_5.utterance: Rescue is here… they're waving us over. Are you going? I'll follow you.
day_5.response:
Yeah. I'm going.

Come on, let's go together.
